chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Kazzaz, from one of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

While we were seated and my father was in the presence of a governor of the Banu Umayya over Medina, my father came and sat down, so he said: 'I was in the presence of this man earlier, and he asked them about the shortening (of prayer). A speaker from them said, 'In three (days)', and a speaker from them said, 'One day and night', and a speaker from them said, 'An early journey (or a short distance).'

So he asked me, and I said to him: 'When the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) received the revelation of the shortening from Jibraeel (peace be upon him), the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) asked him, 'In what distance is that?' He said, 'In a Bareyd (post-stage). He (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'And what is the Bareyd?' He said, 'What is between the shadow of 'Ayr to the shade of Wueyr.'

He (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Then time passed, and the Banu Umayya were seen constructing signs along the road, and they remembered what Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) had spoken of, so they measured what is between the shadow of 'Ayr to the shade of Wueyr, then divided it into twelve miles, so it became three thousand and five hundred cubits for each mile. So they placed the signs. Then when the Banu Hashim became victorious, they changed the matter of the Banu Umayya out of zeal, because the hadith is Hashimite, so they placed beside each sign another sign.'

key_terms.بَرِيد: A post-stage or distance unit (approx. 12 miles)

ai.seo_question: What is the defined distance for shortening prayer during travel according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* traces the jurisprudential origin of the travel distance (*masafat al-qasr*) to the Prophet’s definition of a 'Bareyd' measured between the shadows of mountains 'Ayr and Wueyr. It highlights the historical evolution of this measurement, noting that the Umayyads standardized it to twelve miles (3,500 cubits) for administrative waystations, a metric the Hashimids preserved upon their rise to power, illustrating the interplay between divine revelation, prophetic tradition, and socio-political standardization in Shia fiqh.
